note: Places for Victorian, steampunk and frontier towns. An entry with `eras` is only for those eras; `water` only where the place has that water.

places.summary: A corner public house with etched glass, a snug for the ladies, sawdust in the public bar and a landlord who knows everybody's slate.
A gin palace of mirrors, brass and gaslight, packed on a Saturday night and sorry for itself on Sunday.
The works' pub across the road from the gates, where the shift changes over a pint and a pie.
A riverside pub with a balcony over the water, popular with lightermen and Sunday rowers.
A sailors' pub by the docks with parrots, ship models and a strict rule about knives on the table.
Engineers' pub with a working steam organ, copper-topped tables and blueprints pinned over the bar.
A saloon with swinging doors, a long mahogany bar shipped from back East, a piano player and faro in the back.
Miners' saloon where pay-day comes in dust and leaves in a hurry, with a sign that says check your guns.
A quieter saloon where ranchers and buyers do business over whiskey and cigars, and cowhands are not encouraged.
A modern American bar in the hotel, where bartenders shake strange iced drinks for young men about town.
The town's grand hotel by the station: a palm court, a ballroom, electric bells and waiters in white gloves.
A plain hotel for commercial travellers, with sample rooms, a lounge of newspapers and no liquor whatsoever.
A boarding house run by a widow with strict mealtimes, a parlour piano and opinions about every lodger.
Two storeys of clapboard and a false front, the best beds in town and a dining room that serves the stage passengers.
An old coaching inn that lost its coaches to the railway and now lives on market-day dinners and Saturday dances.
A seafront hotel with a glazed verandah, bathing machines for hire and a band on the lawn in season.
Mutton chops, steak and kidney pudding and stout in high-backed wooden booths, full of clerks at one o'clock.
Plain dining rooms with marble-topped tables, a joint and two veg and a rice pudding for ninepence.
A French restaurant with gilt mirrors and red plush, where the wealthy dine late and are seen to.
Oysters by the dozen, whitebait and a fried sole, standing at the counter or sitting in the back.
A new kind of shop selling fried fish and chipped potatoes wrapped in newspaper, a penny a portion.
Run by a family who came with the railroad crews; noodles, pork buns and the best tea in the territory.
The railroad's eating house, with white linen, a set menu and smart young waitresses who serve a trainload in half an hour.
Tamales, frijoles and green chile stew served off the stove in a whitewashed adobe room.
A restaurant at the top of the mooring mast, with the dining room swaying gently and a view of the airships coming in.
Lace tablecloths, potted palms and a lady trio playing at four, where women may meet without a chaperone.
A temperance coffee room with newspapers on poles, cocoa for a penny and a game of draughts in the window.
One of the new chain tea shops, cheap and clean, with buns and tea for typists and clerks on their dinner hour.
A late-night coffee stall on wheels serving cabmen, constables and anyone else awake at three in the morning.
Bread, pies and a pot of coffee on the stove, and the baker's wife who knows every bit of news in town.
Penny licks, ice cream sodas and a new soda fountain the whole town turns out to try.
A glass-and-iron market hall with butchers, cheesemongers, fruiterers and a tripe stall at the back.
Naphtha flares, barrow boys crying their prices and haggling till midnight for the cheapest Sunday joint.
Flour, nails, coffee, calico, cartridges and mail, all from the same counter, and a stove with chairs round it.
Cold stone floors, ice and porters with baskets on their heads, busy from four in the morning.
Pens and auction rings where the drovers bring the herds, with a market-day pub on every corner.
Flower sellers, a bird market on Sundays and a man who sharpens knives on a treadle wheel.
A new department store with plate-glass windows, lifts, a tea room and floorwalkers in frock coats.
A glass-roofed arcade of milliners, glovers, a music shop and a man who makes clockwork toys.
Bolts of cloth, ribbons and buttons, and a cash railway that whizzes your money to the cashier on a wire.
Where miners bring their ore to be tested and weighed, and where many a dream is found to be pyrite.
Clocks, music boxes and walking brass birds in the window, and a workshop at the back that ticks all night.
Three brass balls over the door; Sunday suits go in on Monday and come out again on Saturday.
Saddles, bridles, chaps and boots, made to measure, with the smell of leather out into the street.
Great coloured carboys in the window, patent pills, scented soap and a chemist who will pull a tooth.
Glass cases of fossils, stuffed birds, a mummy's hand and the town's first fire engine.
Paintings left to the town by a mill owner: Highland cattle, shipwrecks and a great many cows at sunset.
Working steam engines, a calculating engine the size of a room and a lecturer who demonstrates them at noon.
Wax kings, queens and murderers, with a Chamber of Horrors downstairs that costs an extra penny.
The new free library with a reading room of newspapers, a lending library and a librarian who hushes everyone.
Lectures, evening classes and a subscription library for working men improving themselves after the shift.
A subscription reading room in the old assembly rooms, deep in leather chairs and newspapers from back East.
A music hall of comic singers, acrobats and a chairman with a gavel, beer at the tables and a chorus everyone knows.
A gilt and red velvet theatre with a pantomime at Christmas and touring melodramas the rest of the year.
Built by the mine owner to prove the town is civilised; touring companies, lectures and the occasional prizefight.
Balls, concerts and lectures on the wonders of science in a long room with chandeliers.
A shop turned into a cheap theatre, three shows a night of murders and songs for a penny.
A wooden hall where the Saturday night dance brings ranchers in from fifty miles, fiddles going till dawn.
Magic lantern shows, a phonograph that talks and, on special nights, pictures that move.
The parish church, restored in Gothic style, with a surpliced choir, a new organ and a vicar who preaches too long.
A plain brick chapel with a fine choir, tea meetings, a Sunday school treat and very firm opinions on drink.
A white wooden church with a bell shipped round the Horn; preaching on Sunday, school on weekdays, socials on Saturday.
An old adobe mission with thick walls, a cool dark nave and a bell that has rung for a hundred years.
A small synagogue with a carved ark and a congregation that has grown every year since the railway came.
A mission for sailors with a chapel, a reading room, cheap beds and hot cocoa with a sermon.
A new public park with a bandstand, a boating lake, carpet bedding and a drinking fountain given by the mayor.
A seafront promenade of iron railings and shelters, crowded on Sundays with families in their best.
A garden cemetery of angels and obelisks laid out like a park, where people walk and picnic on Sunday afternoons.
A square of cottonwoods round the courthouse, with benches, a bandstand and a horse trough.
A rough field with goalposts, a cinder path and a hut where the cricket club keeps its roller.
Glasshouses of palms and orchids, a fernery and a lily pond, with a curator who names every plant in Latin.
Rows of allotments with sheds, rhubarb, prize leeks and old men who know exactly what you are doing wrong.
Gardens with coloured lamps, a dancing platform and fireworks on summer Saturday nights.
Irrigated rows of apple and peach trees beside the ditch, with a stand selling cider in the fall.
The square with the town hall clock, the statue of somebody's grandfather and the cabmen's shelter.
The main street of false-fronted stores, wooden sidewalks and hitching rails, ankle-deep in dust or mud.
Cabs, porters, newsboys and the station clock everyone sets their watch by.
A town hall with a clock tower taller than the church, built to show the neighbouring town who is richer.
An iron pier on stilts with a pavilion at the end, penny slot machines and anglers along the rail.
The railway viaduct striding over the valley on thirty arches, the town's pride and its favourite view.
A great iron mast where the mail airships tie up, with a lift to the top and crowds watching every arrival.
A chimney two hundred feet high, the tallest thing for miles and the town's weather vane by its smoke.
The adobe army fort the town grew up around, half of it now a store and the other half still the army's.
The mine's tall timber headframe and stamp mill, thumping day and night so the whole town feels it.
A white lighthouse on the point, with a keeper who lets visitors up the stairs on Sunday afternoons.
Steamers and sailing ships alongside, cranes, bonded warehouses and dockers waiting at the gate for the call-on.
Narrowboats tied up three deep, a toll house and horses resting at the trough while their boats load coal.
Where the river steamer ties up twice a week, with half the town down to see who gets off.
The drifters land herring by the cran, and the gutting girls work at the troughs singing.
The blacksmith and livery stable, where horses are shod, wagons mended and the latest news is hammered out.
The newspaper office and job printers, clattering presses at night and the editor's pistol in the drawer.
A photographer's studio with painted backdrops, a head clamp to keep you still and portraits in the window.
Barrel makers hammering hoops in a yard of staves, for the brewery, the fish quay and the gunpowder works.
A watchmaker with a loupe screwed in his eye, mending pocket watches and setting the town's clocks.
Vast sheds where airship envelopes are stitched and the gasbags tested, with rigging lofts up in the roof.
Public baths with a first- and second-class plunge, slipper baths for washing and a gala every summer.
Dumb-bells, Indian clubs, a vaulting horse and a sergeant-instructor who barks at clerks.
A sparring room above a pub where amateurs learn the noble art and professionals take their money.
A boathouse of polished shells, a regatta in June and a lot of young men in striped blazers.
The town's cricket ground with a pavilion, a scoreboard boy and a Saturday crowd that has seen better.
The professional football club's ground, with a wooden stand, a mud pitch and ten thousand on a cup day.
The racecourse on the heath, with a grandstand, bookmakers shouting the odds and a crowd of every class.
A fenced arena and grandstand where the roundup ends in bronc riding, roping and a county fair.
The canal towpath out past the locks into fields, where courting couples and anglers go on Sunday.
A road up onto the moor above the smoke, where whole families walk on bank holidays for the air.
A trail up the dry canyon to a spring and a rock with every courting couple's initials scratched into it.
A cliff path with a shelter halfway, a camera obscura at the end and a view of every ship in the bay.
A long beach with bathing machines, donkey rides, Punch and Judy and a man selling shrimps by the pint.
A vast glass pavilion with palms, a ballroom and a band, for the days when the seaside is too wet.
Steam roundabouts, swingboats, coconut shies and a fat lady, on the field by the river every autumn.
An exhibition of the age's wonders: an analytical engine, a steam carriage and a mechanical chess player.
A veterinary surgeon for the town's carriage horses, cattle and dogs, with a forge in the yard.
